processing: Organic black tea, described by a retailer as biodynamic; withered, rolled, oxidised and fired as usual for its class.
harvest_season: Picked through the year; as elsewhere in Uva, the dry-weather quality season is generally most valued.
appearance_dry: Dark brown to black broken leaf, typical of Uva grades such as BOP.
appearance_liquor: Clear, bright reddish amber, typical of high-grown Uva.
taste_profile: As with other high Uva teas, expect a brisk, bright cup with a clean finish; the organic label says nothing by itself about flavour.

brewing.notes: Western-style; a broken grade such as BOP needs a shorter steep, around three minutes.

vintage_note: Sold under the estate name by specialist retailers, with organic certification on the label. As usual for Ceylon, it is not a vintage tea: buy recent manufacture and drink within a year or two.
description:
Idulgashinna, also spelled Idalgashinna, is an organic tea garden in the Uva country near Haputale, listed among Stassen's plantations. What sets it apart is less a particular taste than its organic farming.

The leaf goes through standard black tea making, with organic and biodynamic farming being the difference.

Expect the character typical of high Uva, brisk and bright. Brew it Western-style with water just off the boil, and take a little off the time for broken grades, which turn sharp quickly.

You will see several spellings when shopping, so search for all of them, and check the certification on the pack.
history: Accounts of its beginnings are thin: one retailer says it began as a tea estate in 1984, was certified organic in 1989 and has been biodynamic since 1999. These dates come from a tea seller, not from independent records.
